tagline: Lion mountains above an Atlantic harbor
overview:
Sierra Leone curves along the Atlantic coast of West Africa, a country about the size of South Carolina wedged between Guinea and Liberia. Its name comes from Portuguese sailors who in the 1400s called the hills above the shore Serra Leoa, the lion mountains, perhaps for the thunder that rolls off them in storms. The capital, Freetown, sits on one of the world's largest natural harbors, its houses climbing steep green slopes above the water.

About 8 million people live in Sierra Leone. English is the official language, used in schools and government, while nearly everyone talks in Krio, a language built from English and African languages that lets the country's many ethnic groups understand one another. Sierra Leone is a republic with an elected president. Farming, fishing and mining drive the economy, and the country's diamonds are famous around the world. South of the capital, beaches of white sand run for miles below forested hills.
landAndNature: Mangrove swamps and sandbars line the coast, giving way inland to rolling forest and savanna and rising in the northeast to Mount Bintumani, about 1,945 meters high. The rainy season from May to October is drenching, and Freetown is among the wettest capital cities in Africa. Tiwai Island, a research reserve in the Moa River, has one of the densest populations of primates on Earth, including the rare pygmy hippopotamus, which is roughly the size of a large pig and hides in rainforest streams. Chimpanzees, forest elephants and hundreds of bird species live in the remaining woodland, and sea turtles nest on the beaches.
peopleAndCulture: The Mende in the south and the Temne in the north are the largest of about sixteen ethnic groups, and Muslims and Christians live side by side, often within the same family. Rice is the heart of every meal, served with cassava leaf stew, groundnut soup or fried plantain, and pepper is used generously. Palm wine is tapped straight from the trees. Masked dancers, drummers and storytellers perform at harvests and ceremonies, and gumbe and bubu music keep villages moving. Soccer is the national passion, played barefoot on the beaches at low tide, and Krio proverbs season everyday conversation.
history: Farming peoples settled these forests thousands of years ago. Portuguese traders arrived in the 1400s, and for centuries the coast became a departure point for the transatlantic slave trade. In 1787 British campaigners against slavery founded a settlement for freed people that grew into Freetown, later home to thousands rescued from slave ships by the Royal Navy; their descendants became the Krio. Britain ruled the country as a colony until independence on April 27, 1961. From 1991 to 2002 a brutal civil war tore the country apart, funded partly by diamonds and marked by attacks on civilians and the use of child soldiers. Peacekeepers helped end it, an Ebola epidemic struck in 2014, and Sierra Leone has rebuilt in peace since.
funFacts: Freetown's harbor is one of the largest natural deep-water harbors in the world, big enough to shelter whole fleets of ships.
The Star of Sierra Leone, dug up in 1972, weighed about 969 carats and is among the largest diamonds ever found.
A giant cotton tree stood for centuries in the middle of Freetown as a national symbol until a storm brought it down in 2023.
Pygmy hippos weigh about a tenth as much as common hippos and live alone in the forest rather than in herds.
Krio, spoken by almost everyone in Sierra Leone, grew out of English mixed with West African languages and is understood far beyond the country.
